List I describes four systems, each with two particles $A$ and $B$ in relative motion as shown in figure. List II gives possible magnitudes of their relative velocities (in $m{s}^{- 1}$) at time $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}s$.

List-I List-II
(I)

$A$ and $B$ are moving on a horizontal circle of radius $1m$ with uniform angular speed $\omega = 1rad{s}^{- 1}$. The initial angular positions of $A$ and $B$ at time $t = 0$ are $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ respectively.

 (P) $\dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2}$
(II)

Projectiles $A$ and $B$ are fired (in the same vertical plane) at $t = 0$ and $t = 0 . 1s$ respectively, with the same speed $v = \dfrac{5\pi}{\sqrt{2}}m{s}^{- 1}$ and at $45 °$ from the horizontal plane. The initial separation between $A$ and $B$ is large enough so that they do not collide, $\left(g = 10m{s}^{- 2}\right)$.

 (Q) $\dfrac{\left(\sqrt{3} - 1\right)}{\sqrt{2}}$
(III)

Two harmonic oscillators $A$ and $B$ moving in the $x$ direction according to ${x}_{A} = {x}_{0}sin\dfrac{t}{{t}_{0}}$ and ${x}_{B} = {x}_{0}sin\left(\dfrac{t}{{t}_{0}} + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ respectively, starting from $t = 0$. Take ${x}_{0} = 1m, {t}_{0} = 1s$.

 (R) $\sqrt{10}$
(IV)

Particle $A$ is rotating in a horizontal circular path of radius $1m$ on the $xy$ plane, with constant angular speed $\omega = 1rad{s}^{- 1}$. Particle $B$ is moving up at a constant speed $3m{s}^{- 1}$ in the vertical direction as shown in the figure. (Ignore gravity.)

 (S) $\sqrt{2}$
(T) $\sqrt{25{\pi}^{2} + 1}$

Which one of the following options is correct?
options: $I \to R, II \to T, III \to P, IV \to S$
$I \to S, II \to P, III \to Q, IV \to R$
$I \to S, II \to T, III \to P, IV \to R$
$I \to T, II \to P, III \to R, IV \to S$
questions.solution:
(I)

Angular velocity of both the particles is same. Therefore, angle between them will remain $90 °$.

$\left|{v}_{rel}\right| = \sqrt{2}\omegaR = \sqrt{2}m{s}^{- 1}$

Hence, $I \to S$

(II)

The velocity of A at any time t can be written as

${v}_{A}\left(t\right) = \dfrac{5\pi}{\sqrt{2}}cos45 ° \overset{^}{i} + \left[\dfrac{5\pi}{\sqrt{2}} \times sin45 ° - g \times t\right]\overset{^}{j}$

$= \dfrac{5\pi}{2}\overset{^}{i} + \left(\dfrac{5\pi}{2} - gt\right)\overset{^}{j}$

Velocity of B at any time t

${v}_{B}\left(t\right) = \dfrac{- 5\pi}{2}\overset{^}{i} + \left(\dfrac{5\pi}{2} - g\left(t - 0 . 1\right)\right)\overset{^}{j}$

Relative velocity at time t will be,

$\overset{\to}{v}rel = 5\pi\overset{^}{i} - g \times 0 . 1\overset{^}{j}$

$\left|\overset{\to}{v}rel\right| = \sqrt{25{\pi}^{2} + 1}m{s}^{- 1}$

Hence, $II \to T$

(III)

Relative position of A wrt B can be written as

$x = {x}_{A} - {x}_{B}$$= {x}_{0}sint - {x}_{0}sin\left(t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

Using trigonometric relation

$x = \sqrt{2}{x}_{0}sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$

Therefore,

${v}_{rel} = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \sqrt{2}{x}_{0}cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$

at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$

${v}_{rel} = \sqrt{2}cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$$= \sqrt{2} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2}m{s}^{- 1}$

Hence, $III \to P$

(IV)

The velocity of A is in $xy$ plane and it is $\left|{v}_{A}\right| = \omegar = 1m{s}^{- 1}$ and the velocity of B is along $z$ axis and $\left|{v}_{B}\right| = 3m{s}^{- 1}$. Therefore,

${v}_{rel} = \sqrt{{3}^{2} + {1}^{2}} = \sqrt{10}m{s}^{- 1}$

Hence, $IV \to R$

questions.q: A point charge $q$ of mass $m$ is suspended vertically by a string of length $l .$ A point dipole of dipole moment $\overset{\to}{p}$ is now brought towards $q$ from infinity so that the charge moves away. The final equilibrium position of the system including the direction of the dipole, the angles and distances is shown in the figure below. If the work done in bringing the dipole to this position is $N \times ( mgh )$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, then the value of $N$ is ____________ (Note that for three coplanar forces keeping a point mass in equilibrium, $\dfrac{F}{sin\theta}$ is the same for all forces, where $F$ is any one of the forces and $\theta$ is the angle between the other two forces)
questions.solution:
$W = qV + mgh$

$= q\left(\dfrac{kp}{{x}^{2}}\right) + mgh . . . \left(1\right)$

For equilibrium

$\dfrac{qE}{sin\beta} = \dfrac{mg}{sin\left(90 - \dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)}$

$\dfrac{qE}{sin ( 180 - \alpha )} = \dfrac{mg}{cos\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)}; \dfrac{qE}{sin\alpha} = \dfrac{mg}{cos\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)}$

$\dfrac{9E}{2sin\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)cos\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{mg}{cos\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)}; qE = 2 mg sin\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)$

$q\left(\dfrac{kp}{{x}^{2}}\right) = mgxsin( \dfrac{\alpha}{2} ) = mgsin\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right) \cdot \dfrac{h}{sin\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)}$

$q\dfrac{kp}{{x}^{2}} = mgh . . . \left(2\right)$

From (1) and (2)

$W = 2mgh$

$x = 2$

questions.q: A small particle of mass $m$ moving inside a heavy, hollow and straight tube along the tube axis, undergoes elastic collision at two ends. The tube has no friction and it is closed at one end by a flat surface while the other end is fitted with a heavy movable flat piston as shown in figure. When the distance of the piston from closed end is $L = {L}_{0}$ the particle speed is $v = {v}_{0} .$ The piston is moved inward at a very low speed $V$ such that $V < < \dfrac{dL}{L}{v}_{0},$ where $dL$ is the infinitesimal displacement of the piston. Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct?
options: The rate at which the particle strikes the piston is $\dfrac{v}{L}$
After each collision with the piston, the particle speed increases by $2V$
The particle's kinetic energy increases by a factor of $4$ when the piston is moved inward from ${L}_{0}$ to $\dfrac{1}{2}{L}_{0}$
If the piston moves inward by $dL,$ the particle speed increases by $2v\dfrac{dL}{L}$
questions.solution:
Therefore change in speed $= \left(2V + {V}_{0} - {V}_{0}\right)$
$= 2V$
In every collision it acquires $2V ⇒ \left(B\right)$ is correct

Now, frequency of collision of particle with piston,
$⇒ f = \dfrac{V}{2x}$ (as it has to travel $“2x”$ distance with speed $“V”$ ) $⇒ \left(A\right)$ is incorrect
Acceleration $⇒ \dfrac{dv}{dt} = f \times 2V$
$⇒ dv = \dfrac{V}{2x}2Vdt$
$dv = \dfrac{V}{2x}2\left(- dx\right)\left(asVdt = - dx\right)$
$\mathop{∫}_{{V}_{0}}^{V}\dfrac{dv}{v} = \mathop{∫}_{l}^{x}\dfrac{- dx}{x}$
$⇒ ln ⁡ \dfrac{V}{{V}_{0}} = - ln ⁡ \dfrac{x}{l}$
$⇒ V = \dfrac{{V}_{0}l}{x}$
where $x = \dfrac{l}{2}, V = 2{V}_{0}$
$∴ {K}_{i} = \dfrac{1}{2}m{V}_{0}^{2}$ and ${K}_{f} = \dfrac{1}{2}m{\left(2{V}_{0}\right)}^{2} = 4 . {K}_{i}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{K}_{f}}{{K}_{i}} = 4 ⇒ \left(C\right)$ is correct.

questions.q:
A thin and uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ is held vertical on a floor with large friction. The rod is released from rest so that it falls by rotating about its contact-point with the floor without slipping. Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct, when the rod makes an angle ${60}^{o}$ with vertical?
[ $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity]
options: The radial acceleration of the rod's center of mass will be $\dfrac{3g}{4}$
The angular acceleration of the rod will be $\dfrac{2g}{L}$
The angular speed of the rod will be $\sqrt{\dfrac{3g}{2L}}$
The normal reaction force from the floor on the rod will be $\dfrac{Mg}{16}$
questions.solution:
Using conservation of energy
$∆ K + ∆ U = 0$
$\dfrac{1}{2}{I}_{0}{\omega}^{2} = - ∆ U\left({I}_{0} = momentofinertiaaboutHinge\right)$
$\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{m{l}^{2}}{3}{\omega}^{2} = - \left(- mg\dfrac{l}{4}\right)$
$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{3g}{2l}} ⇒ \left(C\right)$ is correct
$⇒ {a}_{radial} = {\omega}^{2} . \dfrac{l}{2} = \dfrac{3g}{2l}\dfrac{l}{2} = \dfrac{3g}{4} ⇒ \left(A\right)$ is correct
Now, $τ = I . \alpha$
$⇒ mg . \dfrac{l}{2}sin ⁡ 60 = \dfrac{m{l}^{2}}{3} . \alpha ⇒ \alpha = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}g}{4l}$
$⇒ \left(B\right)$ is incorrect
Acceleration in vertical direction $⇒ {a}_{v} = \left(\alpha\dfrac{l}{2}\right)sin ⁡ {60}^{o} + {\omega}^{2}\dfrac{l}{2}cos ⁡ {60}^{o}$
$= {a}_{v} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}g}{8}\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{3g}{8}$
${a}_{v} = \dfrac{9g}{16} + \dfrac{6g}{16} = \dfrac{15g}{16}$
Now, using $NLM ⇒ mg - N = m{a}_{v} ⇒ N = mg - m{a}_{v} = mg - \dfrac{15}{16}mg$
$⇒ N = \dfrac{mg}{16} ⇒ \left(D\right)$ is correct

questions.q: A particle is moved along a path $AB - BC - CD - DE - EF - FA,$ as shown in figure, in presence of a force $\overset{\to}{F} = \left(\alphay\overset{^}{i} + 2\alphax\overset{^}{j}\right)N,$ where $x$ and $y$ are in meter and $\alpha = - 1N / {m}^{- 1} .$ The work done on the particle by this force $\overset{\to}{F}$ will be ____ Joule.
questions.solution:
$dw = \overset{\to}{F} ⋅ d\overset{\to}{r}$
$dw = aydx + 2axdy$
Now, total work done in whole path is given by,
$W = {W}_{AB} + {W}_{BC} + {W}_{CD} + {W}_{DE} + {W}_{EF} + {W}_{FA}$
$A \to B, y = 1, dy = 0, {W}_{A \to B} = ∫ \alphaydx = \alpha ⋅ 1\mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}dx = \alpha$
$B \to C, x = 1, dx = 0, {W}_{B \to C} = 2\alpha ⋅ 1\mathop{∫}_{1}^{0.5}dy = - 2\alpha\left(0.5\right) = - \alpha$
$C \to D, y = 0.5, dy = 0, {W}_{C \to D} = \mathop{∫}_{1}^{0.5}\alphaydx =\alpha ⋅ \dfrac{1}{2}\mathop{∫}_{1}^{0.5}dx = - \dfrac{\alpha}{4}$
$D \to E, x = 0.5, dx = 0, {W}_{D \to E} = 2\alpha ∫ xdy = 2\alpha ⋅ \dfrac{1}{2}\mathop{∫}_{1}^{0.5}dy = - \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$
$E \to F, y = 0, dy = 0, {W}_{EF} = 0$
$F \to A, x = 0, dx = 0, {W}_{E \to A} = 0$
$∴ W = \alpha - \alpha - \dfrac{\alpha}{4} - \dfrac{\alpha}{2} = - \dfrac{3\alpha}{4}$
Given $\alpha = - 1 ⇒ W = + \dfrac{3}{4}J = 0.75J$

questions.q:
In the List-I below, four different paths of a particle are given as functions of time. In these functions, $\alphaand\beta$ are positive constants of appropriate dimensions and $\alpha \ne \beta$ . In each case, the force acting on the particle is either zero or conservative. In List-II, five physical quantities of the particle are mentioned: $\overset{\to}{p}$ is the linear momentum, $\overset{\to}{L}$ is the angular momentum about the origin, K is the kinetic energy, U is the potential energy and E is the total energy. Match each path in List-I with those quantities in List-II, which are conserved for that path.
LIST -I LIST-II
A) $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alphat\overset{^}{i} + \beta\overset{^}{j}$ P) $\overset{\to}{p}$
B) $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alphacos ⁡ \omegat\overset{^}{i} + \betasin ⁡ \omegat\overset{^}{j}$ Q) $\overset{\to}{L}$
C) $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alphacos ⁡ \omegat\overset{^}{i} + sin ⁡ \omegat\overset{^}{j}$ R) $K$
D) $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alphat\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{\beta}{2}{t}^{2}\overset{^}{j}$ S) $U$
T) $E$
questions.solution:
$( i )$ $\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right) = \alphat\overset{^}{i} + \betat\overset{^}{j}$
$\overset{\to}{v} = \dfrac{d\overset{\to}{r}\left(t\right)}{dt} = \alpha\overset{^}{i} + \beta\overset{^}{j}$ {constant}
$\overset{\to}{a} = \dfrac{\overset{\to}{dv}}{dt} = 0$
$\overset{\to}{P} = m\overset{\to}{v}$ (remain constant)
$k = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}$ {remain constant}
$\overset{\to}{F} = - \left[\dfrac{∂ U}{∂ x}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{∂ U}{∂ y}\overset{^}{i}\right] = 0$
$⇒ U \to$ constant
$E = K + U$
$\dfrac{d\overset{\to}{L}}{dt} = - \overset{\to}{τ} = \overset{\to}{r} \times \overset{\to}{F} = 0$

A particle of unit mass is moving along the x-axis under the influence of a force and its total energy is conserved. Four possible forms of the potential energy of the particle are given in column I (a and ${U}_{0}$ are constants). Column I Column II

B. ${U}_{2}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}{\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}$ Q. The force acting on the particle is zero at $x = 0$ .
C. ${U}_{3}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}{\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}exp ⁡ \left[- {\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}\right]$ R. The force acting on the particle is zero at $x = - a$
D. ${U}_{4}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}\left[\dfrac{x}{a} - \dfrac{1}{3}{\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{3}\right]$ S. The particle experiences an attractive force towards $x = 0$ in the region $\left|x\right| < a$
T. The particle with total energy $\dfrac{{U}_{0}}{4}$ can oscillate about the point $x = - a$
questions.solution:
${U}_{1}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}{\left[1 - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right]}^{2}$
$F = - \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}2\left[1 - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right]\left[- \dfrac{2x}{{a}^{2}}\right]$
$= \dfrac{2{U}_{0}}{{a}^{4}}\left[{a}^{2} - {x}^{2}\right]x$
$F = \dfrac{2{U}_{0}}{{a}^{4}}x\left(a - x\right)\left(a + x\right)$
$F = 0$ , at $x = 0, a, - a$
$\left\begin{array}{ll}x = - a, U = 0, \\ x = 0, U = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}\end{array}\right\} ⇒$ Oscillate when total ME is less then $\dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}$
$A \to P, Q, R, T$
B- ${U}_{0}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}{\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}$
$F = - \dfrac{{U}_{0}x}{{a}^{2}}$
$F = 0, x = 0$
$B \to Q, S$
C- ${U}_{3}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{U}_{0}}{2}\left[{\left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)}^{2}exp ⁡ \left(- \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}\right)\right]$

$x = 0, x = - a, x = + a, F = 0$
$x = 0, U = 0$ even function hence minima
$C \to P, Q, R, S$

$x = + a, x = - a, F = 0$

$D \to P, R, T$

questions.q: A tennis ball is dropped on a horizontal smooth surface. It bounces back to its original position after hitting the surface. The force on the ball during the collision is proportional to the length of compression of the ball. Which one of the following sketches describes the variation of its kinetic energy $K$ with $t$time most appropriately? The figures are only illustrative and not to the scale.
questions.solution:
When ball of mass $' m '$ dropped from height and strikes to ground.It's kinetic energy is converting into elastic potential energy due to compression.

So after time $' t '$ its final velocity,

$v = u + at$

$u$ is initial velocity of ball, $a$ is acceleration of ball and $t$ is time.

$⇒ v = 0 + \left(- g\right)t$

$v = - gt$

Negative sign shows downward direction.

Now kinetic energy of ball,

$K . E . = \dfrac{1}{2}{mv}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}m{\left(- gt\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ K . E . = \dfrac{1}{2}{mg}^{2}{t}^{2}$

$⇒ K . E . ∝ {t}^{2}$

So, it is upward parabola. But after complete compression, $K . E .$ becomes zero, then ball will reshape again. Kinetic energy will not be constant.

questions.q:
Statement I A block of mass $m$ starts moving on a rough horizontal surface with a velocity $v$. It stops due to friction between the block and the surface after moving through a certain distance. The surface is now tilted to an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal and the same block is made to go up on the surface with the same initial velocity $v$. The decrease in the mechanical energy in the second situation is smaller than that in the first situation.
Statement II The coefficient of friction between the block and the surface decreases with the increase in the angle of inclination.
options:
Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is a correct explanation for Statement I

Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is NOT a correct explanation for Statement I

Statement I is true, Statement II is false

Statement I is false, Statement II is true
questions.solution:
In statement I Decrease in mechanical energy in case I will be
$$
\Delta U_1=\frac{1}{2} m v^2
$$
But decrease in mechanical energy in case II will be
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Delta U_2=\frac{1}{2} m v^2-m g h \\
& \Delta U_2 < \Delta U_1
\end{aligned}
$$
$$
\therefore \quad \Delta U_2 < \Delta U_1
$$
or Statement $\mathrm{I}$ is correct.
In Statement II Coefficient of friction will not change or this Statement is wrong.
$\therefore$ Option (c) is correct.
